64-086.r: Bacteriophages → viruses that infect and replicate in bacteria; used as vectors in genetic engineering to transfer DNA (both true).

64-087.r: Mouse grown about eight times bigger using a human growth hormone gene → technique is genetic engineering.

64-088.r: DNA testing in crime investigation → samples can be blood cells, bone cells, hair strands, saliva (all four), also semen.

64-089.r: DNA fingerprinting (Alec Jeffreys; variable minisatellites) → proves paternity and criminal identity; trace hair, saliva, dried semen suffice (A and R true, R explains A).

64-090.r: Basis of DNA fingerprinting → DNA polymorphism (highly variable non-coding regions differ person to person); used to prove paternity and identity.

64-095.r: First crime solved using DNA fingerprinting → England: rape and murder of two teenagers in 1983 and 1986 (answer: 1983).

64-096.r: Biometric identification → iris scan, retinal scan and voice recognition (all three), besides fingerprint, face, DNA, palm print, gait.

64-097.r: Developing fingerprints on multicoloured (and nonporous: plastic, glass, metal) surfaces → fluorescent powder.

64-098.r: NOT achieved by transgenics → cloned animals (cloning is separate); transgenics give biodegradable plastic, edible vaccines, transgenic crops.
64-098.t: Transgenesis = inserting a foreign gene; cloning = making genetically identical copies.

64-099.r: Change in base sequence within a gene → mutation (permanent change in DNA sequence).

64-100.r: Pleiotropy → one gene controls two or more characters at once (e.g. phenylketonuria, albinism, sickle cell anaemia).
64-100.h: Pleio = many: one gene, many effects.

64-101.r: Gene therapy → introduces a normal copy of a gene into cells to make up for a faulty one. The book gives no single answer (*).

65-001.r: MicroRNA → discovered 1993 by Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun; 2024 Nobel Prize (Physiology/Medicine) for it and post-transcriptional gene regulation.

65-002.r: AYUSH = Ayurveda, Yoga and Naturopathy, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy (six Indian systems of medicine); earlier the Department of ISM&H, formed 1995.

65-003.r: Red Ribbon Express → moving (train) medium for HIV/AIDS awareness: transmission, prevention, risk.

65-004.r: Sanraksha → AIDS research and control project, Bengaluru (began as HIV counselling service, 1993).

65-005.r: Avahan → Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation initiative to reduce spread of HIV/AIDS in India; began 2003.

65-006.r: NACO (National AIDS Control Organisation, 1992) → division of Health Ministry; nodal body for HIV/AIDS policy and control in India.

65-007.r: Mission Indradhanush (MoHFW, 25 December 2014) → full immunisation of children under two and pregnant women against seven vaccine-preventable diseases.
65-007.h: Indradhanush = rainbow: seven colours ↔ seven diseases.

65-010.r: Anaemia Mukt Bharat → iron and folic acid (not calcium) supplements; delayed cord clamping campaign; periodic deworming; non-nutritional causes (malaria, haemoglobinopathies, fluorosis) → three correct.
65-010.t: Supplement is iron-folic acid, not calcium.

65-011.r: National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission → launched 1 July 2023 at Shahdol (MP) by PM Modi; target: eliminate sickle cell anaemia by 2047.

65-012.r: National Programme for Control of Blindness → 1976; ICDS → 1975; National Leprosy Eradication Programme → 1983; National Rural Health Mission → 2005.

65-013.r: NFHS-5 did NOT include an HIV test; it covered high blood pressure, diabetes, death registration, pre-school education.

65-014.r: Wrong pair: Washing soda – potassium; washing soda is sodium carbonate (Na2CO3). Correct: chlorophyll–magnesium, haemoglobin–iron, table salt–sodium (chloride).

65-015.r: Vinegar → acetic acid; souring of milk → lactic acid; bones → calcium phosphate; gastric juice → hydrochloric acid (HCl).

65-016.r: Milk to curd → bacteria ferment lactose (milk sugar) into lactic acid, which gives the sour taste.

65-017.r: Bones → calcium phosphate; vinegar → acetic acid; souring of milk → lactic acid; ripening of fruits → ethylene.

65-018.r: Skin cancer → ultraviolet rays; noise pollution → decibel; global warming → carbon dioxide (CO2); ozone hole → chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).

65-019.r: Wool → biodegradable (made of keratin protein, like human hair); plastic cups, glass bottles, aluminium foil are not.

65-020.r: Biodegradable waste → turned into useful substances (compost, humus, methane) mainly by bacteria (also yeast and fungi).

65-021.r: Insecticides → non-biodegradable pollutant; paper, food and plant waste, wood and cellulose are biodegradable.

65-022.r: Lactobacillus → curd; Rhizobium → nitrogen fixation; Yeast → alcohol production; Aspergillus → citric acid formation.

65-023.r: Industries widely use bacteria, microalgae and fungi (bacteria: curd, cheese, vinegar, antibiotics; diatom algae: diatomaceous earth for glass, filters).

65-024.r: Methanogens (a group of archaebacteria) → produce methane as by-product in low-oxygen (hypoxic) conditions.

65-025.r: Toddy fermentation → Saccharomyces (a yeast genus of fungi).

65-026.r: Commercial ethanol → yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae (baker's yeast), which prefers fermentation to respiration.

65-027.r: Wine industry fermentation → yeast; turns grape-juice sugars into alcohol, with carbon dioxide (CO2) as by-product.

65-028.r: Microbes can grow above boiling point (hyperthermophiles 80-110°C, some survive above 121°C), below freezing point, and at pH below 3 → all three true.
